title: Big Tech Is Destroying Democracy. Here’s How to Fight Back.
gist: Ravi Agrawal interviews Nobel laureate Maria Ressa, co-chair of the UN Scientific Panel on AI, who argues that Big Tech and AI agents are eroding democracy and that the US-China 'AI race' framing is narrative warfare. She cites a 75-80% global drop in news-site traffic from generative search, says 53% of internet traffic is non-human, and says the advertising business model for journalism is dead.

insights.claim: Maria Ressa frames AI's societal rollout in three phases: social media micro-targeting about a decade ago, LLM chatbots from 2022-23, and now agentic and multi-agent systems that hack human agency itself.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Shifts regulatory focus toward agentic AI, where liability and permission frameworks are still unsettled.
insights.quote: Now what’s being hacked is agency itself. You literally give these agents permission to act for you.
insights.locator: These three stages hacked our biology

insights.claim: Ressa says the UN Scientific Panel on AI's July preliminary report concluded the technology is not controllable, after the release of Mythos and Fable 5 and the July 'Hugging Face incident'.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
entities: UN Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence
insights.so_what: An official UN body calling frontier AI uncontrollable raises the odds of multilateral regulation and headline risk for AI developers.
insights.quote: In July, when we released the preliminary report from the Scientific Panel on AI, we told you that this is not controllable.

insights.claim: Ressa says LLMs have never been factual because they are probabilistic machines, and chatbots have moved the information ecosystem toward 'AI slop'.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Reliability concerns underpin pressure for content-integrity rules affecting AI product design.
insights.quote: LLMs have never been factual—they’re probabilistic machines.

insights.claim: The UN AI panel, with members from 36 countries and about a quarter from Big Tech, produced its preliminary report in six weeks; Ressa says the friction was between people and Big Tech rather than between the US and China or Russia.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Signals cross-bloc consensus on AI principles is achievable, which could accelerate global AI standards.
insights.quote: Where we tore our hair out was between people versus Big Tech, but we found consensus.

insights.claim: Ressa calls the US-China zero-sum AI race framing 'narrative warfare' used to justify skipping safeguards, and urges people not to believe it.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Challenges the core rationale for light-touch US AI policy; if the framing loses traction, regulatory risk for AI firms rises.
insights.quote: First, it’s narrative warfare. Don’t believe it.

insights.claim: The United States voted against creating the UN scientific panel on AI, which Ressa says shows the US actively destroying the post-WWII order it helped build.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: US abstention from multilateral AI governance increases odds of a fragmented, non-US-led regulatory regime.
insights.quote: The United States voted against creating the scientific panel.
insights.locator: RA: Tell me how we get

insights.claim: Ressa cites Marietje Schaake's argument that each day governments fail to act on tech, they lose more power, calling it a tech coup that happened in plain sight; even countries without frontier models were told they must regulate to remain able to govern.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Suggests broadening government appetite, including among non-AI-producing states, to regulate platforms.
insights.quote: The tech coup has happened in plain sight. It is time to act.
insights.locator: One of the things I loved in Geneva

insights.claim: A coalition of 20 countries called Democracia Siempre has put information integrity at the top of its agenda, with member Brazil holding elections on Oct. 4.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Information-integrity coalitions may translate into platform regulation in large markets like Brazil.
insights.locator: MR: There are leaders who are fighting

insights.claim: Ressa cites the V-Dem Institute as finding, as of March 2026, that 74 percent of the world lives under authoritarian rule, arguing engagement-maximizing tech is helping elect illiberal leaders democratically.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Rising share of autocratic governance broadens political-risk exposure across emerging markets.
insights.quote: the V-Dem Institute, as of March this year, said 74 percent of the world is now under authoritarian rule.
insights.locator: I’m not speaking as the co-chair

insights.claim: Ressa cites a 2018 MIT study that lies spread six times faster than facts and says the problem worsened after Elon Musk bought Twitter, producing cascading crises of trust, order and accountability.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Framework underpinning regulatory scrutiny of platform algorithms and content moderation.
insights.quote: We know, from a 2018 Massachusetts Institute of Technology study, that lies spread six times faster than facts.
insights.locator: What can you do? In the book

insights.claim: Ressa says she received 11 arrest warrants in 14 months under Duterte, took almost a decade to win 10 of 11 cases, and still needs Supreme Court approval to travel.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Illustrates legal-system weaponization against media in the Philippines.
insights.quote: Over the course of 14 months, I was issued 11 arrest warrants, and it took almost a decade to win 10 of those 11 charges.

themes.theme: Collapse of the news business model

insights.claim: Ressa says generative AI search answers have cut global referral traffic to news websites by around 75 to 80 percent, because AI uses publishers' content without sending readers to their sites.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Structural hit to publisher revenue; strengthens the case for AI content licensing deals and copyright litigation.
insights.quote: The drop globally is around 75 to 80 percent; that’s huge.

insights.claim: Ressa declares the advertising business model of journalism dead, noting Rappler pays for server capacity just so AI scrapers can take its content.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: Publishers face rising costs and falling revenue from AI scraping, pushing them toward paywalls, licensing and anti-scraping tools.
insights.quote: The business model of journalism advertising is dead, and we are looking for the next one.

insights.claim: Ressa states that 53 percent of internet traffic today is non-human and only 25 percent of the internet is the open web, with 75 percent social media and AI.
insights.speaker: Ravi Agrawal
insights.so_what: If accurate, bot traffic dominance undermines ad-measurement integrity and digital advertising pricing.
insights.quote: Fifty-three percent of the internet today is non-human traffic—AI slop.
